newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FEATURE-BRITISH RETAILERS RUSH TO SET UP SHOP IN IRELAND.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-BRITISH RETAILERS RUSH TO SET UP SHOP IN IRELAND.

text.p: A mere 75 years after winning independence from British rule, Ireland is again being invaded by its larger neighbour -- but shopkeepers, not soldiers, are leading the attack.

Drawn by the fastest-growing economy in the European Union and soaring consumer spending, many of the big names in British retailing are at the fore in a stampede to set up shop in Ireland's high streets and shopping centres.
Debenhams, Boots and electrical giant Dixons are among those who have recently opened outlets in Dublin, joining more established retailers like Marks and Spencer, Next and Body Shop in the capital.
DUBLIN A BASE FOR WIDER EXPANSION

For many, getting a toehold in Dublin is just the first step in a nationwide assault, designed to take full advantage of the economic boom which has seen Ireland produce an average growth rate of around eight percent over the last two years.
Boots opened its first store in November in Dublin's new Jervis shopping centre and has plans for another four stores, bringing its total investment in Ireland to 7.6 million pounds ($12.72 million).

"We are delighted to have the opportunity to invest in Ireland at a time when both the economy and in particular, the health and beauty market, are going through a phenomenal growth phase," Boots director of business development, Peter Burdon, said of the company's arrival in Ireland.
Dixon says its Dublin store, which opened in December, is just the first step in a 10 million pound, 300-job expansion.
"We plan to open two more Dixons stores next year and a gradual expansion programme will continue as appropriate sites become available," chief executive John Clare said in December.
The British store group, which has 800 outlets, has just acquired Dublin's Harry Moore chain of six electrical shops which has operated in the capital for more than 50 years.

Meanwhile, Marks and Spencer, in Ireland since 1979, has not been idle. The giant retailer spent 40 million punts ($65.84 million) revamping the old Brown Thomas building on Dublin's busy Grafton Street, turning the 67,000 square feet (6,224 square metres) of retail space into its flagship outlet in Europe.
It also completed a three million punt expansion at its city centre store in Cork.
The group's next move will be to new out-of-town locations with plans for a store at the new Quarryvale centre in west Dublin and another in south Dublin.
It is also looking out for suitable sites in Galway and Limerick as part of a 65 million punt expansion.
CONSUMERS WELCOME NEW ARRIVALS
Unlike previous invaders, the latest British arrivals have been welcomed with open arms by the Irish consumer although the response of Ireland's domestic retailers has been more cautious.
"Retailing is all about consumers and the consumer is the biggest winner with variety and competition," says Declan Martin, economic director of the Dublin Chamber of Commerce.

"The presence of all these people also makes Dublin a more attractive, cosmopolitan European-type city in the sense that there is a far broader choice of shopping and that of course has very positive tourism benefits," Martin told Reuters.

But he says there is some concern among existing Dublin retailers that if the record Irish growth of recent years slows, there could be a shakeout, while there are also worries that there is not greater linkage to the local economy.
"There is a tendency for the truck to come in from the UK, to unload the goods and to be out again within the hour so there's no warehousing and so on," he said.
FEARS NEW BUSINESS MIGHT GIVE LITTLE TO ECONOMY
Others have warned of the threat to sectors such as Irish advertising if the new retailers treat their Irish outlets as if they were merely branches of British chains.
"Companies which enter the Irish market must realise they have a responsibility to use the support services offered by local outfits," warned Ireland's Sunday Tribune.
"It is not good enough merely to ship in all the goods and take the money out, the only contribution to the local economy being the wages and taxes paid."
But generally, Irish retailers accept that competition is inevitable and are braced for a further influx.

The planned Quarryvale shopping development outside Dublin is expected to attract more British retail interest while U.S. fashion outlets like Calvin Klein and The Gap are rumoured to be looking very closely at Dublin.

"You can't block it. It's a free market and it's inevitable with Ireland's economic boom at the moment that people will come into it," Martin says, adding that in terms of Dublin and its economy, the positives definitely outweigh the negatives. ($1=.5974 Pound) ($1=.6075 Punt)
